segments.caption: A model can score well on its own and still not change what clinicians do.
segments.text: A benchmark asks whether the model can answer. A trial asks whether clinicians do better with it. These are different questions, and only the second one decides whether a tool helps patients.

segments.caption: Goh et al. randomized 50 physicians into two groups of 25.
segments.text: Goh and colleagues randomized fifty physicians: twenty-five to G P T four plus their usual resources, and twenty-five to usual resources alone. Both groups worked up to six vignettes in sixty minutes, graded blind on a structured reflection rubric.

segments.caption: Median score per case: 76% with GPT-4, 74% without.
segments.text: The median diagnostic reasoning score per case was seventy-six percent with G P T four and seventy-four percent without. The adjusted difference was two percentage points, with a ninety-five percent interval from minus four to eight and a P value of zero point six zero. The interval includes zero.

segments.caption: Nor was it faster: 519 seconds per case against 565.
segments.text: Nor was it faster. Physicians with the model took five hundred nineteen seconds per case against five hundred sixty-five, a difference of minus eighty-two seconds, with a ninety-five percent interval from minus one hundred ninety-five to thirty-one. That interval includes zero too.

segments.caption: GPT-4 alone scored 92%, 16 points above the control group.
segments.text: In an exploratory arm of three runs, the model alone scored a median of ninety-two percent, sixteen points above the control group. But the physicians who had that same model scored seventy-six. The gap is about how people use the tool, not about the tool.

segments.caption: Each rung of the evaluation ladder answers a question the one below cannot.
segments.text: Benchmark, retrospective study, reader study, prospective trial, then deployment with monitoring. Each rung answers a question the one below it cannot. This trial is the fourth rung, and most published results stop at the first.

segments.caption: A test set of 200 patients: model A is right on 170, model B on 164.
segments.text: A synthetic test set of two hundred patients. Model A is right on one hundred seventy, eighty-five percent, and model B on one hundred sixty-four, eighty-two percent. The question is how much of that three-point gap is just which patients we happened to test.

segments.caption: Draw 200 patients with replacement, recompute, and repeat 10,000 times.
segments.text: The bootstrap answers that by resampling. Draw two hundred patients with replacement, so some appear more than once, recompute the accuracy, and repeat ten thousand times. The spread of those ten thousand numbers is the uncertainty.

segments.caption: The two 95% intervals overlap, and that is not a test of the difference.
segments.text: Model A's interval runs from zero point eight zero to zero point nine zero, and model B's from zero point seven seven to zero point eight seven. They overlap, but overlapping intervals are not a test. Each one answers a question about one model on its own.

segments.caption: The two models were graded on the same patients, so compare them that way.
segments.text: Both models were graded on the same two hundred patients. A is right where B is wrong fourteen times, and B is right where A is wrong eight times. Fourteen minus eight is six patients, which is exactly the three-point difference.

segments.caption: The paired difference is 0.03, with an interval that includes 0.
segments.text: Bootstrapping the difference on the same resampled patients gives zero point zero three, with a ninety-five percent interval from minus zero point zero one five to zero point zero seven five. It includes zero, so these data do not show that A is better. They do not show the models are equal either.

segments.caption: Pairing matters: ignoring it makes the interval two thirds wider.
segments.text: Pairing matters. On the same data, ignoring it widens the interval to minus zero point zero four five to zero point one zero five, about two thirds wider. Report intervals rather than point estimates, and compare models on the same patients.

segments.caption: A model can reach a high score by reading the wrong thing.
segments.text: A model can reach a high score by reading the wrong thing. The score tells you the label came out right. It does not tell you which part of the image produced it.

segments.caption: DeGrave et al. built two datasets, and the second was the favorable case.
segments.text: De Grave and colleagues built two datasets. The first takes positives from GitHub COVID and negatives from Chest X ray fourteen, so source and label line up almost exactly. The second, from B I M C V and Pad Chest, is one region and one research team: the favorable case.

segments.caption: Saliency maps and counterfactuals found it reading the margins, not the lungs.
segments.text: Saliency maps and generative counterfactuals showed what the models used: laterality markers, arrows and text found only in one archive, the radiopacity of the image borders, and patient positioning. Moving the clavicle region to the top border raised the predicted odds of COVID nineteen.

segments.caption: On radiographs from a new hospital system, half the performance was gone.
segments.text: On radiographs from a new hospital system, half of the predictive performance was lost. The authors concluded that only a minority of it was ever genuine COVID nineteen pathology. The rest was the source, not the disease.

segments.caption: Some shortcuts transfer, so passing external validation proves less than it seems.
segments.text: Here is the part that catches people out. Some shortcuts do not transfer, so the score falls and you see it. Others, like patient positioning, are consistent in both datasets: the score holds up and the model is still not reading the lungs. External validation is necessary, not sufficient.

segments.caption: One more way an average lies: it hides the group it works worst on.
segments.text: An average hides the group a model works worst on. Sensitivity of zero point eight five overall can be zero point nine zero in eighty percent of patients and zero point six five in the other twenty. Report subgroups with intervals, validate externally, look at what the model uses, and test whether the site can be predicted from its features.
